description: Create a custom printable ruler or measuring template with adjustable length, metric/inch tick edges, optional center-finding marks, hanging hole, and custom label text. This parametric ruler generator creates a flat, fast-printing measuring reference for workshop layouts, craft projects, school use, notebooks, tool drawers, and quick desk measurements. Customize the measured ruler length, width, thickness, rounded corners, unmeasured end extension, tick style, edge scales, hanging hole, and label text directly in MakerWorld's parametric customizer. Features: - Adjustable measured ruler length, width, and thickness. - Unmeasured end extension so rounded corners sit outside the 0/final marks. - Metric edge scale with mm / 5 mm / 10 mm tick hierarchy. - Inch edge scale with selectable subdivisions. - Top and bottom edge scale selectors: metric, inch, or none. - Raised or engraved tick marks. - Optional raised or engraved numbers. - Optional center-finder marks for layout work. - Optional hanging hole. - Optional custom name/workshop label. - Flat, support-free print orientation. The default is a 150 mm measured ruler with metric ticks on one edge and inch ticks on the other. The physical plate extends slightly beyond the measured span so the rounded end caps are not part of the measurement and endpoint ticks stay supported by straight body material. It includes a hanging hole and center-finder marks; the custom label option is available when you want to add a workshop/classroom name. Important accuracy note: this is a handy printed reference/template, not a certified measuring instrument. Printed accuracy depends on printer calibration, filament shrinkage, slicer scaling, bed adhesion, and first-layer settings. For best results, print a short test, compare against a trusted ruler/caliper, and adjust slicer scaling if your printer is off.

model_name: NASA Titan II Gemini 1:200 Scale Rocket
description: This is a 1:200 scale model of NASA's Titan II GLV (Gemini Launch Vehicle). This rocket was used to launch the Gemini capsule. This rocket, and the program it took off the ground, allowed the United States to test several critical technologies used during the Apollo Program. These tests included multi-crewed missions, orbital rendezvous, docking, spacewalks, and semi-long duration missions. The Gemini program is often overshadowed by the Apollo program, yet it was essential for the apollo's success. To assemble this rocket model you should not need glue. I made the fits tight enough that it can stick on friction alone. All you need to do to put it together is slot the square in between the first stage pieces and slide the second stage onto the mounting pegs. This model was modeled to 1:200 Scale from NASA technical documents and is thus quite accurate in size. This being said, some features and detailing had to be exaggerated to ensure a reasonable printability. This model has a few very detailed sections like the engine section and the exhaust ports. These sections are some of the parts that make the Titan rocket so unique, so I wanted to make them to the best of my ability while keeping them stable enough to print. The model had some very small sections that are prone to breaking and stringing; the hot staging exhaust especially so. It is highly recommended to dry your silver/grey filament as well as running a flow calibration before printing. Even after doing this, my model had a small amount of stringing in this section that I had to carefully cut out with wire snips. I will add a one color test print of only the engines and exhaust ports to help dial in flow rates. I did not change anything model-wise, but my K value and flow rate had to be calibrated. If you have any questions or any future rocket model recommendations please let me know.

INFO These are magnetic separation racks for 0.2mL PCR sized tubes. Works for SPRI, ConA, or any magnetic beads. My lab is a big fan of the epicypher racks but they cost $500 dollars so we were always fighting over the one, and even then when you have more than 8 or 16 samples it is inconvenient to always switch out tubes while doing high through put experiments. I wanted more racks so I designed these with a similar style and functionality to the epicypher racks with some added improvements. 1.Racks come in 8-tube and 12-tube sizes so you can make full use of the multichannel and scale up easier 2.Magnets are removable, so you can simply slide the magnet out rather than removing the tubes from the rack 3.The magnet can be turned around to work better for either small or large volumes. 4. Less than 1% of the price of Epicypher magnet racks (even with the cost of magnets) BEFORE YOU PRINT While smooth, semi-textured, and textured plates all work, I find that printing on a textured plate results in a tighter fit of the magnet holders inside the rack. I prefer the slightly looser fit I get when printing on my BIQU cool plate. If you use my print profile then you don't need any supports, however, these are kind of tall prints so I recommend making sure you have a clean bed and dried filament to avoid any adhesion errors. If you are having adhesion problems then you can take it a step farther and use a cool plate and/or a brim. ASSEMBLY You will need 10x5x3mm magnets. One 8 tube rack takes 16 magnets and one 12 tube rack takes 24 magnets. After printing, glue the two halves of the magnet holder together with the magnet holes in the same orientation. Then, insert the magnets. While they have a snug press fit, I find that they stay in better if the magnets on either side of the holder have opposite poles facing each other (the orientation where they stick together). A dab of super glue doesn't hurt either.

description: The STEM MicroLaunch Rocket is a hands‑on chemistry experiment disguised as an awesome mini rocket. Designed for classrooms, STEM clubs, home learning, and curious kids everywhere, this project demonstrates how a simple chemical reaction can generate real thrust. This 3‑part printable kit includes: A micro rocket with internal reaction chamber A dual‑measure scoop (large side for vinegar, small side for baking soda) A snap‑fit launch base Kids measure, mix, assemble, and launch — learning about pressure, gas expansion, and propulsion in a safe, engaging way. Using everyday household ingredients (baking soda + vinegar), the rocket builds up carbon dioxide inside the chamber. When the pressure becomes high enough, the rocket pops off the base and launches upward. It’s a perfect introduction to chemical reactions, Newton’s laws, and basic rocketry. This project is designed for easy printing, simple assembly, and repeatable demonstrations anywhere — in the classroom, at home, or outdoors. The included instructions guide users step‑by‑step through measuring, loading, launching, and cleaning the rocket after use. Instructions 1. Using the smaller scoop, add 1 full small scoop of baking soda into the rocket base. 2. Using the large scoop, add 1 full large scoop of vinegar into the rocket. 3. Quickly push the base onto the rocket firmly . 4. Set the rocket down in an open space, then stand clear for launch. Do not lean over the top of the rocket !!! Base Fit & Launch Technique The launch base is tapered slightly — thinner at the top and wider at the bottom. This design helps accommodate small tolerance differences between printers and makes it easier to place the rocket onto the base smoothly. When securing the rocket onto the base, start with light pressure . If the rocket doesn’t build enough pressure to launch, increase the pressure slightly until you find the “sweet spot” where the rocket seals well, builds CO₂ pressure, and launches cleanly. Placing the rocket down too firmly can cause it to get stuck and not launch. If this happens, please seek help from an adult. The adult should hold the rocket upside down , then gently press the base from each side. This will cause the base to pop off with the same force the rocket would have launched — so make sure it is pointed away from people, pets, or objects . For best results, try to place the rocket as evenly as possible onto the base so all sides have equal pressure. It may take a little practice, but once you get the feel for it, the STEM MicroLaunch Rocket launches beautifully and travels a surprisingly good distance for such a small rocket. How It Works The chemical reaction between baking soda and vinegar creates a rapid build‑up of carbon dioxide gas. As pressure increases inside the rocket, the gas escapes through the base, creating thrust and launching the rocket upward. Warnings & Safety Read and follow all instructions Securely install the base before launching Only launch outdoors in a safe open space Powerful thrust — never lean over the rocket Eye protection recommended Move away from the rocket when launching Tips & Maintenance Clean the rocket thoroughly after use so the vinegar doesn’t corrode the parts The fuel will splash — wear clothes you don’t mind getting wet

A simple gear set I created for a maker day event at the library. I would have preferred to just use something that was already out there, but as is typical for me, I began to want certain features / tweaks, so I just made my own. These were modeled in TinkerCAD using the gear generator shape. I wanted: something small and simple and lite for kids a grid / board that supports a large number of combinations of gear connections a way to drive the gears without turning them by hand an indicator for direction they were turning Ended up with: 5mm spaced grid board Works with 10T, 12T, 18T, 20T, 21T, 24T, 30T, 31T, 40T gears (most perfectly, some combinations have a tiny spacing error) Small hole direction indicator Handle / driver PDF activity for kids (8+) I initially didn't want to use pegs and fully open pegboard holes because I wanted the gears to be standard with hole in the center and no attached peg. So I initially started with a true board of pegs for gears to slip onto, but then realized I would be very limited with gear placement without some deep hubs on the gears to clear the peg heights. So then I moved onto a design with gears that slotted onto removeable pegs with separate c-clips to keep them on (like @osamutake models). The pegs screwed into slots on the board and then c-clips locked the gears onto them. This worked, but then I realized it wasn't so simple for kids, and the print resolution would have to be very fine to ensure threads were clean and c-clips were strong enough for kids to not break them. Kids screwing pegs in and out of the board and snapping c-clips into place, especially if the prints weren't perfectly clean, was going to be a problem.. So finally I reluctantly accepted a pluggable gears design into a holed pegboard as posted (similar to design by @Ioannis Tsar). The grid spacing evolved from 10mm to 5mm to support more gears. Also evolved from a hexagonal shape to conserve space and keep diagonal distances equilateral, but then the 5mm hypotenuses worked even with small spacing errors, so kept the grid shape for simplicity. The handle didn't work great and could be redesigned. This was my 3rd design, but still not driving the gears as well as hoped. Could definitely benefit from redesign. I had to print about 100 pieces of everything (sans 40T gears), so needed fast prints. Profile defaults to Random seam so seam is less of a hurdle. A grid bound at 0% sparse infill, draft 0.24mm layer print worked fine for me for my event. Gears were printed with 10% infill. A few posts snapped if kids were rough, so consider higher infill for longer lasting model. Sanding posts definitely helps but is time consuming. I would only recommend if you wanted to keep the kit around for a long time. If it's a one-off event, the gears work fine once snapped in and turned a bit.

My Educational Mechanical Examples Series This model is one of my educational mechanical mechanism examples on 80mm x 80mm base plates. You can find all models of the series in this collection => [Mechanical Mechanism Examples] The present model This is an educational model of Bennett's Linkage, which is a popular 3d four-bar linkage. Brief Description Bennett's Linkage, invented by Geoffrey Thomas Bennett in 1903, is a four-bar linkage that operates in three dimensions; in the standard configuration shown here, the rotational axis of each joint is perpendicular to the link it connects, but the two axes at the ends of a single link are not parallel—they are skew to each other. As a result, the linkage moves out of the plane during its motion. A three-dimensionally operating four-bar linkage of this kind is, in fact, very unusual . This stands in striking contrast to the four-bar linkages oparating in a plane , which are the most fundamental of all link mechanisms. For a planar linkage (in which all rotational axes are perpendicular to the plane), three links simply form a rigid triangle, while four links allow each vertex to trace a well-defined trajectory, with one bar fixed. With five links, the system has excess degrees of freedom and the trajectories are no longer determined. For a general linkage that is not confined to a plane, the number of degrees of freedom is given by the Grübler–Kutzbach formula : Here, N is the number of links, j is the number of joints, and fi is the number of degrees of freedom of the i -th joint. This formula can be read as follows: One of the N links is held fixed, leaving ( N - 1) free links. Each free link has six degrees of freedom in three-dimensional space: three for its position ( x , y , z ), two for the direction in which the bar points (latitude and longitude on the sphere of directions), one for the rotation about the bar's own axis (which sets the orientation of the joint axes at its two ends). A rigid joint removes the equivalent of one full link's worth of degrees of freedom, namely six. If a joint has internal degrees of freedom rather than being rigid, those degrees of freedom are retained. Substituting N = 4, j = 4, and fi = 1 (rotational joint) gives a value below zero. This means that if the link lengths and joint axis directions are chosen arbitrarily, the linkage cannot move—indeed, it cannot even be assembled. In two dimensions, by contrast, each free link has only three degrees of freedom: two for the position of the bar ( x , y ), one for its orientation in the plane. The formula accordingly becomes and for the same four-bar case it gives M = 1. A single parameter is therefore just enough to specify the trajectory of each vertex. Mechanisms that move despite a zero or negative mobility count M ≦ 0 are called overconstrained mechanisms . Although the formula suggests they should not move or even not be assembled, careful choices of link lengths and axis directions can cause the constraints imposed by the joints to become degenerate. The effective number of independent constraints is then reduced, and a working linkage with M = 1 can be realized. Bennett's Linkage achieves M = 1 by recovering three degrees of freedom through the following geometric conditions: Here, the four links are connected in a closed quadrilateral and numbered 1 through 4 cyclically, with ai denoting the length of the i -th link. Each link carries a rotational joint at each end, and the rotational axes are perpendicular to the link itself. The two axes at the ends of a single link are not parallel, however, but make an angle θi with each other. The first and the third linkages share exactly the same configuration and the second and the fourth do, too. In this particular model, θ 1 = 90° and θ 2 = 30° were chosen. Twice per cycle, the linkage passes through a configuration in which all four bars line up along a single axis. Straight bars would collide at this instant, so the actual links are given a cranked shape that displaces their bodies sideways while leaving the joint axes in their correct geometric positions. Bennett's Linkage is a theoretically fascinating system in which a non-trivial degeneracy among the constraints yields exactly M = 1. While it does not have many widely familiar everyday applications, it is being studied for use in deployable structures for spacecraft, and specialized hinges. A similar idea applies to camera pointing. Flip the model and imagine that a camera is mounted on the back of the base plate, as in the youtube video, then hold the central bar steady with one hand and rotate the base plate with the other. The camera's line of sight traces a closed curve in space, and combined with the camera's own field of view, a single Bennett linkage can cover a useful angular range with just one actuator. References https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overconstrained_mechanism Case This model is compatible with the case included in my first set . Printing Use the models named ???-printable.stl for printing . The models named ???-assembled.stl are provided just to show how they should be assembled. Use well-dried PETG to have better dimensional accuracy. Use 0.1 mm or 0.08 mm layer height to have smoother surfaces. Use slow printing speed for overhangs. Select “Random” seam position to have smoother rotation. Randomly distributed seam should be easily worn out after some wearing.Printing Sanding and Filing Note that, in this model, the rotation of the bases for bearings is intentionally made not too smooth. Sometimes, the gears suffer from the stringing effect and/or elephant foot effect, resulting in a too tight fit to the shafts (they are designed with a 0.15 mm radial clearance). If you see rough surface on the shafts due to stringing, sand off the roughness with a small piece of sand paper. If you feel the gears do not rotate smoothly due to an elephant effect, widen the hole slightly by using a thin round bar file. Without those issues, the parts should rotate very smoothly with minimal friction. Assembly Just secure the joints by the retaining rings. Pinza Multiuso Gommata (Scala 1:4) | Meccanismo Articolato Porta la vera ingegneria sulla tua scrivania! Questo non è un semplice giocattolo, ma la riproduzione in scala 1:4 di una vera " Pinza Multiuso Gommata " industriale, basata su un efficiente meccanismo a ginocchiera. La Storia del Progetto 🎓 Ho progettato questo cinematismo per un progetto di Laboratorio di Progettazione Meccanica in Università. La versione reale (in scala 1:1) è stata rigorosamente dimensionata e verificata dal punto di vista strutturale per sollevare in totale sicurezza carichi fino a 10 kN (circa 1 tonnellata). Ho deciso di scalarla in formato 1:4 per permettere a tutta la community di testare con mano la cinematica e la fisica dietro questo tipo di macchinari: più l'oggetto da sollevare è pesante, più la forza di serraggio orizzontale delle ganasce aumenta! (Per i più curiosi e gli appassionati di meccanica, ho allegato tra i file anche la mia relazione di calcolo originale completa di verifiche e dimensionamenti in lingua italiana). Dettagli di Stampa Ho caricato il profilo .3mf completo e già ottimizzato per BambuStudio. Il progetto è completamente stampabile in 3D , inclusi tutti i perni di articolazione (non avrete bisogno di viti o ferramenta esterna). Materiali: PLA o PETG per la struttura principale. Stampa Multimateriale SENZA AMS (Il trucco per le ganasce): Nel piatto dedicato alle ganasce ( Jaws ), ho impostato una pausa strategica prima degli ultimi layer. Questo vi permetterà di cambiare manualmente la bobina anche se non avete un AMS. Potete usare del filamento nero per un semplice contrasto estetico, oppure caricare del TPU . Usare il TPU per i primi strati simulerà il vero cuscinetto in gomma industriale, garantendo il giusto attrito per afferrare e sollevare davvero gli oggetti sulla vostra scrivania! Guida al Montaggio 🔧 (Screenshot) Le Chele Principali: Iniziate unendo le due chele centrali tramite il perno di articolazione mediano. I Bracci Superiori: Collegate le bielle alla parte superiore della struttura, posizionando l'anello di sollevamento (cruna) al centro ed i relativi perni. Le Ganasce: Agganciate le due ganasce inferiori (quelle con la presa gommata) ai bracci esterni e collegatele con i rispettivi perni. Nota sui perni: Inserite tutti i perni stampati in 3D nei rispettivi occhielli per chiudere il cinematismo (I perni più lunghi colleganmo gli elementi portanti della pinza, mentre quelli più corti collegano le chedle della pinza con le risepttive ganasce gommate). My planned launchpad area was on concrete, which doesn't work well with printable stakes, so I decided to redesign the bottom of the leg to reduce the size of the stake hole to support mounting to a heavier wood base with a screw and washer. It also makes putting the launcher at an angle much safer, if you are going for distance or competing with the wind. Later we took the setup to a large park, and the launcher was instantly set up and secured with the added weight of the base. The print profile includes a plate that uses a modifier part to increase the infill around the mounting hole. I printed one without this reinforcement and it worked perfectly, but for an extra 3 minutes and less than a gram of filament, you get a little extra insurance against over tightening your screw and crushing the walls of the print. This is by far the best launching system I have seen, and it was quick and efficient to print. Highly recommended. With these updated feet mounted to a heavy base, setup is quick and easy, regardless of location.

I wanted to electroplate my models and investigated online for suiting models. Found none that I was happy with. So I decided to design and build my own. The design consists of three main parts: 1) the motor assembly 2) the controlbox 3) the arc bridge assembly The motor assembly is designed so it can easily be fitted on different sized arc bridges, because not all containers have the same width/height requirements. I will share the dimensions of the current container i used, orderable off amazon. If you have another container, I will share the SCAD file as well, so you can easily adapt the width to your needs. Keep in mind that the min dia is always the width of the motormount plate and standoffs to the side of the container. The motor assembly itself houses the stepper (28BYJ-48) and the ULN2003 motor driver board. The controlbox has a couple of easy to acquire and solder components: an ESP32 board (i used a SEED XIAO ESP32-C6, very small board), a LM2596 buck converter, a rotary encoder (KY-040) to control the speed, a battery and an on/off switch. I will share the scheme here as well. The ESP firmware will also be shared (rename the main.c.txt to main.c) IMPORTANT NOTE; make sure to trim your buck convertor to 5v before connecting anything to it, otherwise it may be set too high and you will fry your electronics The arc bridge is pretty straightforward; it clamps on to the side of the container (dont overdo it, just keeps it from moving around) and comes with a nut to secure the motor assembly in place. Safely observe the Sun by projecting its image onto a translucent screen. This fully 3D printable Solar Projection Screen is designed for standard 1.25" (31.75 mm) telescope eyepieces and provides a bright, comfortable image that can be viewed by several people simultaneously. It is ideal for astronomy outreach, schools, science clubs and public observing sessions. Unlike traditional solar projection systems, this design features a removable screen cassette . Besides allowing the tracing paper to be replaced in seconds, the cassette can also be inserted into different positions inside the projector to adjust the projection size , allowing you to choose the best compromise between image brightness and image size. The entire assembly is mechanical. No screws, no glue and no additional hardware are required. Features Compatible with all standard **1.25" (31.75 mm) telescope eyepieces Fully 3D printable Threaded connection between the projector body and eyepiece adapter No screws No glue No additional hardware Removable screen cassette Easy replacement of the projection screen Adjustable projection size by changing the cassette position Compact and lightweight Optimized to minimize support material Ideal for astronomy outreach and educational demonstrations Required Parts Besides the printed parts, you only need: One standard 1.25" telescope eyepiece One sheet of tracing paper (vellum) Cut the tracing paper to: 112 × 110 mm No other parts are required. Printing Recommendations Recommended material eSUN PETG+HS This model has been designed and successfully tested using eSUN PETG+HS (High Speed) filament. PETG is strongly recommended because the projector is exposed to direct sunlight during use. PLA is NOT recommended , as prolonged exposure to sunlight may soften or deform the printed parts. Recommended print settings Layer height: 0.20 mm Nozzle: 0.4 mm Supports: Minimal (body only) Brim: Not required The geometry has been carefully optimized to minimize support material , making printing easier while reducing post-processing. Assembly Cut the tracing paper to 112 × 110 mm . Open the screen cassette. Insert the tracing paper. Close the cassette until all clips engage. Slide the 1.25" eyepiece into the eyepiece adapter. Insert the eyepiece and adapter assembly into the telescope focuser. Tighten the focuser thumbscrews to secure the eyepiece. Screw the projector body onto the eyepiece adapter. Slide the screen cassette into the desired position. The projector is now ready for use. Using the Projector For safe operation and optimal performance, an aperture mask is strongly recommended . An aperture of 50 to 80 mm is generally sufficient to obtain a bright, high-contrast solar image while significantly reducing the thermal load on the telescope and the projector. Fit the aperture mask to the front of the telescope, keeping the aperture cover closed . Install the projector on the telescope. Once the projector is securely installed, remove the aperture cover to expose the reduced aperture. Point the telescope toward the Sun using a safe solar finder or by minimizing the telescope's shadow. Focus using the telescope focuser. Observe the projected solar image on the screen. The removable screen cassette can be inserted into different positions to adjust the projection distance. Shorter projection distance: brighter image. Longer projection distance: larger projected solar image. Safety ⚠ NEVER look through the eyepiece while this projector is installed. This accessory is designed exclusively for solar projection . An aperture mask is strongly recommended to reduce the amount of solar energy entering the telescope and to limit heat buildup. Always supervise the telescope while it is pointed at the Sun. Never leave the telescope unattended. This projector does not replace a certified solar filter intended for direct visual observation. Design Highlights Designed specifically for FDM 3D printing, this projector combines ease of printing with practical field use. Highlights include: Threaded connection between the projector body and eyepiece adapter Removable screen cassette Adjustable screen position Quick replacement of the tracing paper Compact design Effective internal light shielding Geometry optimized to minimize support material Reliable and straightforward assembly No screws, glue or additional hardware Inspiration This project was inspired by two well-known solar projection systems: Baader Planetarium – Solar Projection Screen The Sun Funnel ( https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WXpAyN_cul4 ) Rather than reproducing these designs, this project is a complete redesign focused on: full 3D printability, compatibility with standard 1.25" telescope eyepieces , adjustable projection size, removable screen cassette, compact dimensions, elegant appearance, assembly without screws, glue or additional hardware, compact and support-efficient construction. !!!!! Hinweis bitte vor dem Drucken die kompette Beschreibeung lesen !!!!! Dieses Getriebe ist Teil eines Projektes aus der Vorlesung Konstruktionslehre IV aus unserem Studium. Ich habe das Getriebe zusammen mit @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas und zwei anderen Kollegen entwickelt. Wir haben dies zusätzlich zu der Ausarbeitung abgegeben und sind mächtig stolz darauf. Es ist ein wunderbares Anschauungsmodell, welches weiter optimiert wurde als die ursprüngliche abgegebene Version. Hier die wichtigsten Infos zum Getriebe: - das Planetengetriebe ist Teil eines Antriebstranges einer Presse. Um das Getriebe herum befindet sich noch ein deutlich größeres Schwungrad, sowie eine Kupplung. - ich habe das Getriebe komplett aus PLA gedruckt, wie es sich mit anderen Materialien verhält weiß ich nicht - ich habe einen P1S von Bambulab und sehr feine Einstellungen gewählt. Ob das notwendig ist, weiß ich nicht. Das Ergebnis lässt sich aber auf jeden Fall sehen - ich würde das Getriebe nicht skalieren, da sich sonst Abstände zwischen Lager und Welle proportional erhöhen, diese jedoch aufeinander abgestimmt sind - Für ein komplettes Getriebe muss man die Platten 1-3 und 4 oder 5 drucken. Die Platte 4 enthält einen Ständer mit Fläche für ein Schild (Siehe in der pdf), die Platte 5 ein Ständer ohne Fläche für ein Schild. - nach meiner Farbkodierung ist: weiß die Antriebswelle, schwarz der Abtrieb von Planetenträger, grau das Gehäuse, rot die Zahnräder, grün die Lager und gelb der Stopfen bzw. die Schrauben - ich habe folgendes geklebt: die Stifte in das Gehäuse, den Stopfen in das Gehäuse, die inneren Lager, direkt am Gehäuse - die Deckel können auf das Gehäuse geklebt werden, dann kann das Getriebe jedoch nicht mehr auseinandergenommen werden. Damit das Getriebe trotzdem zusammenhält ist die Klammer da. Diese kann von unten auf das komplette Gehäuse geschoben werden - die Kleinen Lager gehen lassen sich nur sehr schwer in die Zahnräder pressen. Dafür diese vorsichtig mit etwas diese in die Zahnräder schlagen, bis die Lager deutlich unter der Kante des Zahnrades sind - der Deckel vom Planetenträger hat extra eine Aussparung, sodass man ein Zahnrad sieht. Die „Schrauben“, welche Wirklichkeit nur Stifte sind, gingen bei mir sehr schwer. Wenn ihr das Getriebe wieder gut aufmachen können wollt, diese am besten ein wenig kleiner Skalieren und evtl. an den Deckel vom Planetenträger kleben - das angehängte pdf enthält die Beschriftung (52mmx22mm), ich habe dies auf Papier (DIN A4) ausgedruckt, welches man als Aufkleber verwenden kann. Es lässt sich aber auch mit normalem Papier ausdrucken und aufkleben - das ganze Getriebe mit Gestell braucht ca. 130g Filament - ich habe für die Stützen unter dem Gehäuse ein paar Schichten Support for PLA verwendet. Wenn kein Support for PLA Filament vorhanden ist dies einfach zu PETG ändern. Das funktioniert genauso. (Wenn das Getriebe aus PETG gedruckt wird dann zu PLA wechseln) Daher kommen auch ein paar wenige Filamentwechsel. Wer dies möchte einfach das Profil normale Stützen drucken. Ich habe insgesamt 5 Modelle gedruckt bis das Getriebe die finale Version hattte. Viel Spaß damit! english version: This gearbox is part of a project from the “Design Engineering IV” course in our degree program. I developed the gear together with @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas and two other colleagues. We submitted this in addition to our term paper and are incredibly proud of it. It’s a wonderful demonstration model that has been further optimized beyond the original version we submitted. Here’s the key information about the gearbox: - The planetary gearbox is part of a press’s drive train. Surrounding the gearbox is a significantly larger flywheel, as well as a clutch. - I printed the gearbox entirely out of PLA; I don’t know how it would behave with other materials. - I used a Bambulab P1S and selected very fine settings. I’m not sure if that was necessary. In any case, the result is definitely impressive. - I wouldn’t scale the gearbox, as doing so would proportionally increase the distances between the bearings and the shaft, which are designed to be precisely matched. - To build a complete gearbox, you need to print plates 1–3 and either 4 or 5. Plate 4 includes a support with space for a label (see the PDF); plate 5 includes a support without space for a label. - According to my color coding: white is the drive shaft, black is the output shaft of the planetary carrier, gray is the housing, red is the gears, green is the bearings, and yellow is the plugs or screws - I glued the following parts in place: the pins into the housing, the plug into the housing, and the inner bearings directly to the housing - The covers can be glued to the housing, but then the gearbox can no longer be taken apart. The clip is there to keep the gearbox together anyway. It can be slid onto the entire housing from below - The small bearings are very difficult to press into the gears. To do this, gently tap them into the gears with a small tool until the bearings are clearly below the edge of the gear. - The cover of the planetary carrier has a special cutout so you can see a gear. The “screws”—which are actually just pins—were very difficult for me to insert. If you want to be able to open the gearbox easily again, it’s best to scale these down slightly and possibly glue them to the cover of the planetary carrier - The attached PDF contains the label (52mm x 22mm); I printed this on paper (DIN A4), which can be used as a sticker. However, you can also print them on regular paper and stick them on. - The entire gearbox with the frame requires about 130g of filament. - I used the Super Cool Track Pro plate for the housing and the Textured PEI Plate for the rest. That’s how it’s set up. If you use different plates, be sure to take this into account! - I used a few layers of “Support for PLA” for the supports under the housing. If you don't have “Support for PLA” filament, simply switch to PETG. It works just the same. (If the gearbox is printed in PETG, switch to PLA.) That's why there are a few filament changes. description: 我们设计并建造了PrintScope——一种可3D打印、制造极其简单、低成本的显微镜，旨在为任何人开启通往微观世界的大门。 在设计之初，我们调研了网上各种各样的显微镜方案，其中著名的Foldscope项目给了我们极大的启发。Foldscope本质上是一种列文虎克式显微镜——通过一颗极小的玻璃珠提供很大的曲率，作为单片式超级放大镜来观察样本。它有着像场不平、观测距离很近的先天局限，但也同时拥有成本低廉、超级便携的突出优点。 Design Background 我们买来Foldscope进行测试后，发现它仍存在一些实际痛点：网购一套的成本约20元，它使用了特殊的高弹性卡纸并进行了预裁切，如果完全用唾手可得的A4纸复刻，不仅加工费时，精度和性能也大打折扣；同时，那颗玻璃珠如何稳固地固定在纸面上也是一个棘手的问题。此外，Foldscope需要裁切出机台、X轴滑动台、Y轴滑动台、装片夹、镜头卡扣、斜坡等七八个零件，学习成本相当高。 于是我们开始思考：有没有可能进一步降低物料成本？有没有可能大幅降低手工复刻的学习成本？在3D打印机逐渐普及、打印变得前所未有的容易的当下——我们能不能做出一款基于3D打印的、谁都能通过创客类网站下载文件并自行复刻的简易显微镜？ 于是，PrintScope 诞生了。 作为iGEM竞赛团队的成员，我们在合成生物学实验中，常常需要快速观察细菌、酵母和植物组织样本。传统的实验室显微镜虽然精密，但笨重、昂贵，难以带到课堂、户外或科普活动现场。这款PrintScope正是我们为教育场景和iGEM outreach活动量身打造的工具——让每一位学生、爱好者，甚至资源匮乏地区的孩子们，都能亲手看到那个曾经只存在于课本里的微观世界。 Main Features 在光学系统设计上，我们沿用了列文虎克/Foldscope式的单片式构造。我们从网上购买了多种不同直径的玻璃珠（1mm、1.5mm、2mm、4mm等）通过光学公式定量计算焦距、放大倍率、工作距离等核心参数，完整对比数据见下表（表1），以此完成多规格透镜系统性测试，发现2mm玻璃珠是最优的折中选择。 结合参数分析：若选用 1mm 玻璃珠，理论放大倍率可达 333×，但仅 0.25mm 的工作距离空间极狭小，标本很难放置、调试难度极高；4mm 及更大直径玻璃珠的工作距离充足，但放大倍率大幅衰减（4mm 仅 83×），观测细节表现力不足；2mm 玻璃珠有效倍率约 167 倍，工作距离（样品到镜头的距离）约0.5mm，既保留充足放大倍率，又预留出适配常规生物标本的操作空间，兼顾成像效果与装配、调阅的易用性 —— 更大直径珠子倍率不足，更小直径珠子则因工作距离过窄难以安装、观察。 基于此，我们将整个显微镜优化为仅需两个3D打印部件：镜体底座和弹性卡扣式镜片座（FlexiLens）。并针对Foldscope的痛点做了以下针对性优化： 一体化卡扣式镜体——无需胶水、无需额外零件，轻松拼装，仅需2个打印件 滑轨式对焦——通过手指捏住两侧princhbridge按压桥，带动中间Flexi Origami折纸结构的FlexiLens柔性调焦片形变，可轻松实现精准对焦 图2 图3 图4 图5 调焦滑轨：组装卡扣和pinchbridge左半（图2）、pb右半边和组装好的调焦滑轨（图3）（与实际左右对应） fl的最低/最高两种状态：最低（图4）、最高（图5） 四向辅助观察口——上下左右四个方向开设样品居中观察孔，方便快速将样本定位到透镜中心 手指适配槽与推片凹槽——左侧向内凹试区域适配大拇指，增加了手动控制装片位置的范围和调整灵活性 图6 四向辅助观察口、拇指适配区域与按压方式解析（图6） 左右对称设计——同时适配左撇子和右撇子用户 人体工学持握设计——镜体背面的凹凸结构经过精心优化，刚好适配食指的自然弧度；使用时一手持握，另一手推动载玻片调焦，调焦动作完全在侧面进行，不遮挡视线，无需反复调整眼睛位置即可舒适观察 图7 背面适应食指结构（图7） 图8 图9 推荐两种观察方式：（观测前建议摘下眼镜，获得更清晰的成像效果） ①一手捏显微镜，一手捏装片，对准灯光/天空观测（图8） ②手机手电筒作为光源（亮度最低），贴近桌面进行观察（图9） 兼容标准载玻片——学校实验室现有耗材直接可用 图10 图11 支持标准化玻璃装片：图10、图11（红色槽位即给标准载玻片的适配位图） 极致轻量化——适合课堂分组、户外采样、科普路演 优化弹性结构——耐得住多次折叠，且整个装置仅使用PLA Basic即可打印，无需弹性TPU材料，进一步降低门槛 Components Included 底座：稳定支撑，中间圆孔为透光通道，让自然光照亮样本。· 载片：放置观察样本的平台，中间小孔为弹珠镜头安装位，四周小孔辅助透光。· 弹珠镜头：核心放大部件，安装在黑色载片中间小孔，实现显微成像。 Assembly Notes 1.将载片平稳卡入底座的卡槽中，确保中间透光孔对齐。 2.把高透明弹珠卡入载片中心的小孔内，固定牢固即可。（建议将弹珠静置于桌面，载片正面朝下，中心小孔对准弹珠下压） 注意事项： 1.本支架依靠 0.2mm 超薄柔性铰链实现弯折夹持，禁止暴力大幅度反复弯折，过度扭曲会造成铰链断裂、永久折痕发白，碎片易划伤手指；若出现开裂、破损请立即停用，不要继续使用破损支架夹持镜头与标本。 2.本品为PLA塑料制品，易软化，请勿放置窗台、暖气、台灯等高温光源旁以免变形 3.配套生物切片为薄玻璃载玻片，玻璃边缘锋利，拿取、插入支架滑槽时捏住标签区域，禁止直接触碰玻片切割边缘，防止割破皮肤； 4.装载玻片时平缓推入支架卡槽，勿用力硬塞，防止玻片受力崩裂；观测完成后先取出切片，再收纳支架，不长期将玻璃片卡在支架内挤压存放。 5.优先使用室内柔和自然光透射观测，若使用台灯补光，灯具与支架保持 10cm 以上距离，强光、近距离长时间照射会加热支架 PLA 结构，造成软化变形；禁止使用激光、强光手电直射镜头与人眼，强光会损伤视网膜。

This is my Astronomy Without Borders Onesky 130F5 upper tube assembly. I found two major deficiencies with the original upper tube assembly. The sloppy threads in the helical focuser, that does not have adequate rigidity The finicky secondary mirror collimation The sloppy threads in the original helical focuser is well known with kludgy fixes like wrapping the threads in Teflon tape or using grease on the threads… But the bigger problem was the thin plastic cantilevered design. If you tried using any moderately heavy eyepieces the weight was cause it to sag and vibrate intolerably at higher magnifications, making planetary observing incredibly frustrating. And for some reason that I can not imagine, people making these entry level telescopes put the spring between the secondary mirror and the hub thingy. When you loosen the locking screw the whole thing just goes wherever it wants and makes collimation a total pain. Also, having the whole assembly on the one round rod made one more axis it could rotate on and need adjusting. Very annoying. In this upper tube assembly, the whole things is printed thick and solid, allowing for the mounting of a full size Crayford focuser. This upper assembly is very solid and has very little deflection. It uses a four vane spider, and I relocated the spring to the top side of the hub so it's in a push/pull orientation. Now when you loosen the center screw a turn or two, the spring holds the mirror mount against the three screws so you can actually see what effect your adjustments have on your collimation. As an added benefit, the holes for the strut rods are much deeper, which leaves a lot less unsupported rod length further increasing stiffness. And finally, I rotated the focuser around a bit for easier seated observing. IMO, the stock orientation seemed better for standing and hunching over the telescope. Now the focuser is at a 45° angle which I think offers better ergonomics. There are a couple of compromises though. First, it makes the telescope very top heavy. I had to slide the dovetail all the way as far as it can go, and it's still not 100% perfectly balanced but it's good enough. And second, the large Crayford sticks out axially further than the original focuser, requiring the use of 22mm spacers limiting how far the telescope extends to achieve focus. This is the focuser: https://agenaastro.com/gso-crayford-focuser-reflector-telescope-dual-speed-eaf-1-25.html Use the 176mm base curvature option. The design also utilizes this dovetail mounting shoe https://a.co/d/0iBxRjiH It is designed for m6 screws but I wanted to only use M4 on this design so I made this insert that allows the use of two M4 x 16mm countersunk head screws.` The designed it to use 4mm heat set inserts. https://a.co/d/0dv4AGsl Finally, I purchased this red dot finder scope https://a.co/d/04XIdzyd My only criticism is that even on the dimmest setting it's still pretty bright. I printed all the parts in ABS at 0.16mm layers, 6 wall loops, 20-25% gyroid infill with 3 fill lines. PETG or either ABS or PETG CF would also be nice, but I didn't have that and the normal ABS seems plenty stiff enough. This print requires minimum supports. I would not print in PLA, as it will warp if left in a hot car. I flocked the inside of the telescope tube and shroud, and painted the inside of the upper tube and spider in Musou black paint. https://a.co/d/06kpUJR0 https://a.co/d/05EYCLqY When assembling the strut rods into the upper tube assembly, it's a snug press fit and might require some persuasion with a plastic tipped hammer. The ends of the tubes must be flush with the bottom of the counter-bores. A keen eye will notice the end screws are missing on my telescope. I lost one somewhere along the way but I made the counter-bores a little too tight and makes installing the screw difficult. I fixed this on the uploaded model. I contacted Celestron and Skywatcher for replacement screws but neither were any help, so I'm on my own to find a suitable substitute but it seems like an odd thread. The tube extension fits into a groove and is fixed in place with CA glue. The shroud snaps in firmly, glue is optional. I used a soldering iron set to 280-290C to set the threaded inserts. All finished I could not be happier with the performance of the 'scope. It focuses fast and easy, especially with the Bahtinov mask. The 10:1 micro adjust is a dream. Collimation is easy and holds solidly. Vibrations are minimal and settle quickly.

This radius gauge is specific made for Mitutoyo vernier calipers. There are many simular devices on Makerword but ALL of them have a 45 degree angle. That means you must multiply the mesurement by some weird value. My radius gauge has an angle of 60 degrees. This means that if you mesure a round object then you get exact radius on your caliper. You don't have to calculate anything anymore. Just mesure and you have the exact radius on your caliper display. Disclaimer: This still is a printed pard and can bend while mesuring. If you bend the arms too much your mesurement will deviate. Usage: Puss your Mitutoyo calipers end (for depth mesurement) in the hole of the gauge with the display facing the round indent of the gauge all the way in. Close the caliper to zero. Place your round object against the 2 arms of the radius gauge. Hold the round object and push only the part of the caliper with the display towards the round object untill the pin tuches the round object. Now read the radius of the round object from the screen. This should be half of the outer diameter of the round object. It could be off a little bit because of your printers settings and temperature but my mesurements are realy close. Moon Monitor – Real-time Moon Phase Display A real-time realistic Moon phase display with additional Moon information accessible via a push button. Built with a Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and a 1.28" round TFT display. This is my first project ever with a Raspberry Pi (and with Python). I'm a 50-year-old nerd who still has some potential left — especially with a little help from AI. I originally wanted to build a small aviation radar I saw on my feed. “Where are you right now?” A chunky dial clicks across five feelings, from Calm on the green end all the way up to Explosive on the red. Instead of asking a child to find the words for a big feeling, they just turn the dial and point — nothing needs to be said . A hands-on, non-verbal check-in for calm corners, classrooms, and home — built for self-regulation work, SEND/AAC visual supports, and anger- or anxiety-escalation scales. Features Five clear steps, in escalation order — Calm (green) → Bothered (blue) → Tense (yellow) → Upset (orange) → Explosive (red). Each panel carries its word and a matching face, so it works whether or not the child is reading yet. Red sits on the left and green on the right, so “coming back down” is a move to the right. Built for non-verbal communication. Nobody has to find words: the dial shows where they are. It works when speech won't come — and it's a conversation starter for when it will. A really satisfying click. The dial runs on a printed ratchet with a replaceable spring cartridge — crisp, kid-light clicks in both directions, with a firm “home” at the centre of every zone so the pointer lands square on a feeling rather than between two. THE PANELS ARE INTERCHANGEABLE — BY DESIGN. Each colour lifts out with a fingernail via the notch on the outer rim and snaps back in. Swap a word, re-theme the whole scale, change the language, or replace one scuffed panel without reprinting the body — and more panel sets are available on request: leave a comment with the set you'd like. Click-force options: print the standard cartridge (two dots) or the firmer one (one dot) — they swap in seconds through the hole in the back. Wall-mountable: two keyhole slots (slide down onto the screw heads, which sit flush) or adhesive strips on the flat back. About 207 mm wide. Child-friendly: rounded end corners, no sharp points, and no supports on any part. Print settings PLA, 0.4 nozzle, 0.2 mm layers, no supports anywhere . Body — flat on its back, as exported. Any colour (grey shown). Dial — face-down, as exported. Any colour (grey shown). Cartridge — pick one: standard (2 dots) or firm (1 dot). Flat, any colour. 5 panels — flat, each in its own colour, with a filament change to BLACK Print one panel of each: Explosive (red), Upset (orange), Tense (yellow), Bothered (blue), Calm (green). Assembly (2 minutes, no tools) Cartridge into the pocket on the body's face, nose (the little bump) pointing toward the centre . It push-fits. To get it out again later, poke a rod through the Ø5 hole in the back. Dial — press its shaft into the centre hole until the prongs click home. It then spins freely and clicks both ways. Panels — drop each into its zone and press the edges down. Order left to right: Explosive, Upset, Tense, Bothered, Calm . To remove one, lift at the notch on the outer rim. Mount — two screws (slide the dial down onto the heads) or adhesive strips on the flat back. Notes Designed in OpenSCAD as part of a parametric dial family (2–6 panels, half or full circle). A 3-zone car version and a 16-emotion Feelings Wheel are also available. The wording is deliberately plain — “Bothered” and “Upset” rather than clinical terms — so it can be read by a young child and used in the moment.

When the first rubber band contracts, it pulls its rack and turns the gears. The lever-trigger approach works well here, though other methods (for example bevel or worm gears) could also be used. This high-efficiency mousetrap car is powered purely by the spring mechanical energy of a Windhager mousetrap and utilizes a real gear system to maximize distance. The design runs incredibly smooth and achieved a personal track record of exactly 30 meters! To wind it up, the car must be rotated by three-quarters of a turn at the main gear, featuring a gear ratio of 1 to 64. Required Hardware: 6x 6700 ZZ Ball Bearings (10 x 15 x 4 ) 1x M3 Socket Head Screw 43 mm total length, partially threaded with a 20 mm smooth shank 1x Windhager Mousetrap Step-by-Step Guide: Spring Preparation: Remove the spring from the Windhager mousetrap. Trim the protruding wire ends so that about 2 cm remain, and bend them so they stick out at a 90° angle relative to the spring. Inserting the Spring & Sleeve: Push the printed plastic sleeve inside the spring. Then, insert the spring into the main motor cavity of the chassis with the thicker side of the spring facing inward. Main Gear & Core Screw: Place the large main drive gear onto the spring. Pass the M3 screw through the gear and the spring to lock everything into place. Tighten it enough to eliminate wobbling, but ensure it remains loose enough to spin freely without excessive friction. Gearbox Assembly: Press one ball bearing into each of the middle gears. If the fit is tight, gently tap them in using a hammer. Carefully mount these geared assemblies onto their designated pins on the chassis. Axles & Wheel Bearings: Install the axles along with the remaining bearings onto the frame. Tip: For the wheel axles, you can optionally use 3D-printed bearings. However, for the high-load drivetrain gears (Step 4), real metal ball bearings are strictly required! Attaching the Wheels: Finally, press-fit the wheels onto the axles – the large wheels go in the back, and the small wheels go in the front.

model_name: Ostomy Care Training Model Flat & Convex Stoma Set
description: A pair of training models for practicing ostomy barrier and pouch application, designed after observing a gap in clinical training: nurses often place their first barrier directly on a patient, simply because there is nowhere to practice. Commercial simulators exist, but their cost puts them out of reach for many schools and hospitals. The set includes two anatomies: • Flat — the stoma protrudes above a flat surface, where a flat barrier seals correctly. • Recessed — the stoma sits in a depression, the case that calls for a convex barrier, which presses the surrounding skin so the stoma emerges and seals. Choosing wrong between the two is a common cause of leakage and peristomal skin damage. It is a distinction that is easy to state and hard to understand until you have it in your hands. Both models accept standard commercial barriers and pouches, so students can complete the full procedure — measure, cut, apply, check the seal — as many times as needed. ⚠️ Educational training aid only. model_name: 三层化学分子结构挂件合集｜无需 AMS 分层换色
description: 本文旨在介绍一种从化学结构图出发，制作三层分色化学分子钥匙扣的方法。内容涵盖结构确认、矢量绘制、三层轮廓设计、Blender 建模、挂环制作、切片和手动换色等完整流程。 本项目更侧重于分享制作思路和工作方法。使用相同流程，也可以继续制作其他分子结构、化学主题挂件或教学展示模型。 一、确认化学结构 首先选择需要制作的化学分子，并准备一张清晰、可靠的结构式或键线式图片。（在某度即可找到） 制作前需要大致确认以下几点： 化学键的数量和方向 单键、双键和三键 原子符号 显式标注的 H 上标、下标和电荷 支链和官能团 环状结构 立体化学标记 模型外形可以根据打印要求适当加粗，但不能为了美观随意增加、删除或移动化学结构中的信息。 二、绘制三层矢量结构 确认结构后，将化学式重新绘制为三层相互对齐的矢量图形。 这一步最简单建议使用AI， 我会把提示词放到下面。 三层分别为： 1. DETAIL：化学结构层 这一层包含所有需要在正面显示的化学信息，例如： 化学键 元素符号 字母和数字 上标与下标 双键、三键 环状结构 细线和文字需要根据 FDM 打印能力适当加粗，避免切片后消失或打印断裂。 2. ACCENT：中间衬底层 在化学结构层外侧制作连续的随形背景。 这一层的作用是： 承托分散的化学键和文字 将不同结构连接为一个完整零件 提供第二种颜色 增强正面结构的可读性 对于互不连接的文字、支链或原子符号，可以在不影响正面视觉效果的位置加入隐藏连接桥。 3. BASE：底部承力层 在中间层外侧继续扩展轮廓，形成完整底板。 底层主要承担： 整体结构强度 钥匙扣使用时的拉力 第三种颜色 对上方两层的支撑 三层必须保持相同的坐标、比例、方向和中心位置，保证导入 Blender 后能够自然重合。 三、导入 Blender 建模 将三层 SVG 分别导入 Blender，并按照以下顺序处理： 检查三层尺寸和对齐状态。 将SVG挤出0.2mm。 清理重复点和异常面。 分别为三层增加厚度。（BASE层建议2.8mm，ACCENT层建议1.4mm，DETAIL层建议0.8mm，这样刚好就是5mm） 调整三层的 Z 轴高度，使其形成阶梯式分层结构。 将曲线转换为网格。 检查文字、化学键和小孔是否完整。 三层建议分别保留为独立对象，方便后续修改厚度、材质和位置。 四、制作钥匙扣挂环 在结构外缘选择一个受力相对合理的位置添加挂环。 在Bambu Studio切片软件里添加部件 15x15x2.8mm的圆环到合理位置即可。 五、检查打印可行性 建模完成后，需要重点检查以下位置： 最细的化学键是否能够切片 双键之间的间距是否过小 字母内部的小孔是否会被填满 下标数字是否与相邻线条粘连 独立结构是否都有底层支撑 挂环与主体的连接是否足够牢固 三层之间是否存在悬空或重叠 如果某个细节无法稳定打印，应优先整体放大模型、降低打印速度，而不是直接删除化学结构信息。 六、导出和切片 完成检查后，可以将模型导出为 STL 或 3MF，并导入 Bambu Studio 等切片软件。 本模型采用按高度分层的三色结构，因此即使没有 AMS，也可以通过暂停打印手动换料。 基本流程为： 使用第一种耗材打印底层。 在底层与中层交界处添加暂停。 手动更换第二种耗材。 在中层与化学结构层交界处再次暂停。 更换第三种耗材并完成打印。 具体暂停层数应根据模型实际厚度、层高和切片预览确定，不建议只依靠固定层数直接套用。 七、配色思路 为了让三层结构在封面和实物中更清楚，可以使用： 深色底层 高饱和度中层 浅色或高对比度顶层 例如： 深蓝＋湖蓝＋白色 深紫＋紫罗兰＋淡紫 橙色＋金黄＋奶油黄 墨绿＋青绿＋薄荷绿 酒红＋珊瑚粉＋淡粉 顶层化学结构与中间层之间需要保持足够对比，否则文字和化学键在缩略图中不容易辨认。 灵感来源与致谢 本作品受到 MakerWorld 用户 火宅 @user_455577827 发布的 有趣的化学分子挂件（合集） 启发，但由于我的 A1 未配备 AMS，因此我在此基础上探索并制作了一套适用于手动分层换色的三层化学分子钥匙扣流程。 说明 化学结构具有明确的科学含义。制作其他分子时，请尽量使用清晰、可靠的结构资料进行核对，不建议仅凭模糊图片或模型外观推测化学结构。 欢迎使用本方法制作新的化学主题模型，也欢迎分享改进思路和打印结果。

Cylinder, crankshaft, connecting rod & piston: For these components you just need to activate the supports, keep the speed and layer height as in the general settings. Head Cylinder & Carter: For these components, it's best to enable the ironing function for a better surface finish. Go to the quality settings and scroll down to the "ironing" section, select upper surfaces, and set a speed of 20/15 mm/s. Then enable supports and leave the other settings as the general. Pins & Screws: For these components, I recommend enabling variable layer height, so that the threaded parts have higher quality. On the build plate, select a component and click the variable layer height icon in the top-center menu. Then, move the slider all the way to the left toward quality and click adaptive. Then, insert the crankshaft into the bearing hole; this should also require a little effort. Now insert the captive screws into the holes in the crankcase, and insert the cylinder, inserting the screws into the appropriate holes. Now connect the connecting rod and piston by inserting the pin through the holes in the piston and insert them through the top opening of the cylinder. Now you can insert the cylinder head and screw on the nuts. Now connect the connecting rod to the crankshaft by inserting the pin and securing it with the ring. Finally, place the model on the base and secure the back of the crankcase with the screws and nuts. The tolerances of the fits should not require glue, however if your prints will have a different results you can easily use it. description: 36:1 Dual-Stage Planetary Gearbox for NEMA 17 This is a functional 36:1 dual-stage planetary gearbox designed for a NEMA 17 stepper motor. It was developed as a joint reducer for my base-actuated robotic arm, but it may also be useful for other low-speed rotary mechanisms, positioning systems, and experimental robotics projects. This design is the result of a long process of printing, measuring, disassembling, redesigning, and testing. It was not created using nominal CAD dimensions alone. The final geometry was repeatedly adjusted according to the actual behavior of FDM-printed mechanical parts, including: Bore shrinkage Extrusion and outer-wall spread Temperature-dependent dimensional changes Bearing and shaft press fits Deformation caused by assembly pressure Gear-tooth contact Wear during initial running-in One of the most important features is the lower hub of the central sun gear. It was designed as the primary alignment reference between the motor shaft and both planetary stages. Even accurately modeled gears can develop noise, vibration, uneven wear, and backlash when the sun gear is loose, tilted, or eccentric. For this reason, the shaft interface, bearing support, gear clearances, output structure, and six-point fastening system were developed together as one complete mechanical assembly. The gearbox may feel slightly tight immediately after assembly. During controlled low-speed running-in, microscopic high points on the printed tooth surfaces gradually wear away, allowing the gearbox to reach a smoother and more stable final operating clearance. Running-in should only remove minor surface irregularities. Severe binding, tooth skipping, concentrated heating, or large plastic fragments indicate a printing, dimensional, or assembly problem. Demonstration Video https://youtube.com/shorts/FVjSa3sgb2A Main Specifications Gearbox type: Dual-stage planetary gearbox Total reduction ratio: 36:1 Motor interface: NEMA 17 Output method: Upper ring-gear output Main output bearing: 35 × 47 × 7 mm Recommended material: PETG or another strong, dimensionally stable material Intended use: Robot arms and low-speed rotary mechanisms Backlash: Very low perceptible backlash during manual testing Quantified backlash: Not yet measured using calibrated equipment Required Hardware M3 × 20 mm hex socket screws: 6 M3 heat-set inserts, 5 mm height: 24 M3 × 8 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing: 1 M3 × 12 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 M2.5 × 7 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 NEMA 17 stepper motor: 1 Hex-drive screws are recommended for all connections. Important Printing Instructions Use a Brim on All Parts Except the Sun Gears and Planet Gears A brim is strongly recommended for all printed parts except the sun gears and planet gears . This includes: Housing parts Ring gears Output components Bearing retainers Motor-mounting parts Covers and other structural components The brim helps provide: Reliable bed adhesion A stable and flat bottom surface Accurate alignment between stacked housing parts Proper bearing and heat-set insert seating Reduced corner lifting and warping The flatness of the housing, ring gears, and output components directly affects the alignment of both planetary stages. Even a small amount of warping may cause uneven rotational resistance, bearing misalignment, or periodic binding. A brim is not recommended for the sun gears and planet gears because removing it may damage the lower tooth edges or alter the critical tooth geometry. Remove all brims carefully without damaging the bottom reference surfaces. Use the Manufacturer-Recommended Bed Temperature Always use the normal bed temperature recommended for the selected filament. Do not unnecessarily increase the bed temperature to improve adhesion. Excessive bed temperature may cause elephant-foot deformation, which can: Enlarge the lower edges Distort screw-clearance holes Affect bearing and insert locations Prevent stacked parts from seating flat Change the alignment of the planetary stages The first layer must adhere securely without being excessively compressed or spread outward. Use a Strong Material A mechanically strong and dimensionally stable material is strongly recommended. PETG was used during development, but another properly calibrated high-strength material may also be suitable. The selected material should provide: Strong layer adhesion Resistance to cracking Reliable bearing retention Reliable heat-set insert retention Adequate wear resistance Low long-term deformation under bolt pressure and mechanical load Different materials may produce different dimensions, tooth clearances, friction, and running-in behavior. Test the fit carefully before completing the full assembly. Correcting Tight Tolerances When the printed clearances are slightly too tight, first check: Flow ratio First-layer compression Bed temperature Nozzle temperature XY compensation Hole compensation Actual printer dimensional accuracy If excessive material flow or thermal spreading appears to be the cause, printing at a slightly lower nozzle temperature may improve the fit. Reduce the temperature only in small increments. Do not lower it so far that layer adhesion or mechanical strength is reduced. Never Scale or Modify the Model Do not scale the model or change its geometry to correct a fitting problem. Scaling or reshaping the components changes critical mechanical relationships, including: Gear-tooth thickness Gear pitch geometry Planetary center distances Ring-gear engagement Bearing seats Shaft alignment Motor mounting positions Fastener spacing Output concentricity Even a small dimensional change may prevent the two planetary stages from meshing correctly. Do not modify: Gear profiles Gear center distances Bearing locations Shaft interfaces Alignment surfaces Overall component proportions Printing errors should be corrected through printer calibration, flow adjustment, temperature adjustment, first-layer calibration, and appropriate hole compensation—not by changing the model. Assembly Instructions and Precautions Tighten every six-screw pattern gradually in a diagonal sequence. Do not fully tighten one screw before installing and partially tightening the others. Uneven tightening may distort the housing or shift the planetary stages out of alignment. Use moderate hand pressure. Excessive tightening may: Deform the printed housing Distort the bearing seat Misalign the planetary stages Damage or rotate the heat-set inserts Increase rotational resistance Distort the output ring gear If an M3 clearance hole prints too small, carefully open only that clearance hole using a 3.0 mm drill bit so that the screw passes through freely. Do not drill: Heat-set insert holes Bearing seats Sun-gear or planet-gear bores Motor-shaft interfaces Precision alignment surfaces The 3.0 mm drill should only be used on holes intended to provide free passage for an M3 screw. Press the 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing into the housing evenly through its outer ring. Do not hammer the bearing into place, and do not transmit the insertion force through the inner ring or rolling elements. Before applying an external load: Rotate the gearbox by hand in both directions. Check for hard stops or periodic binding. Operate the motor slowly without load. Run the gearbox in both directions. Inspect the teeth and remove loose wear debris. Confirm that the bearing and housing remain properly seated. Increase the load gradually only after smooth operation is confirmed. Stop operation immediately if you observe: Severe binding Tooth skipping Sharp periodic impacts Concentrated heating Large plastic fragments Cracked gear teeth Bearing movement Shaft slipping Rapidly increasing backlash Development Background This gearbox was developed using a printer that I have repaired, modified, and studied for a long time. A newer machine could have produced prototypes faster, but learning the limitations of an imperfect printer taught me how printed parts actually change between CAD, printing, press fitting, assembly, wear, and real operation. I repeatedly printed and measured parts to understand: How internal holes shrink How external surfaces spread How temperature changes the final dimensions How press fitting deforms printed components Which interfaces must remain completely rigid Which microscopic tooth irregularities may safely wear away How initial running changes the final operating clearance The final design represents the complete process: Printing → Measurement → Dimensional correction → Assembly → Running-in → Final operating clearance This is not simply a generic planetary gear set placed inside a housing. The shaft alignment, bearing support, output structure, six-point fastening, gear clearances, and running-in behavior were developed together through repeated physical testing. The precision of this gearbox did not come from a perfect machine. It came from understanding the machine’s limitations and designing around them.

Atmos Mk 1.2 The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a compact 3D-printable model rocket designed for use with Estes E16-6 and E16-8 motors . It features a dedicated electronics bay that can fit a Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico 2 , GY-BME280 pressure sensor , and a 3.7V LiPo battery , allowing makers to add custom flight computers, altitude logging, and other experimental electronics. Designed with accessibility and customization in mind, the Atmos Mk 1.2 can be printed using a wide range of common 3D printing materials. Whether printed in PLA for easy prototyping, PETG for added durability, or other materials for specialized builds, the design can be adapted to suit different launch goals. The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a platform for makers, students, and rocketry enthusiasts who want to explore 3D printing, electronics, and experimental flight systems in a compact and reusable rocket design. Flight Notes Stability margin: Approximately 1.7 calibers . Estimated altitude: Typically reaches 800–1,000 ft (240–305 m) , depending on launch conditions. Flight history: Successfully tested over 3 flights (with a 4th planned) with E16-8 estes rocket motors, demonstrating reliable performance and durable construction, you could use f motors but i wouldn't go below 15N of force engines to ensure safe liftoff. Recommendations: do not attempt to remove the motor directly after flight wait for the plastic to cool read assembly note carefully to prevent hardware issues higher temp materials ensure more durability but i have printed out of both pla and petg for this project and pla will function and work I assembled a flight computer out of a raspberry pi pico a gy bme barometer and a small quadcopter battery for under ten dollars and this platform was mostly designed to test it i encourage others to do the same but also i plan to drop links to my functioning code later once i have it all ironed out Assembly Notes To assemble the Atmos Mk 1.2, you'll need 3–4 pennies, super glue, a nylon or Kevlar shock cord, a small amount of duct tape, recovery wadding, a small i hook, and your choice of recovery system (streamer or parachute) . The rocket is designed for Estes E16-6 or E16-8 motors . The nose cone includes a dedicated ballast pocket: Payload under 15 g: Glue 4 pennies into the nose cone. Payload over 15 g: Glue 3 pennies into the nose cone. For the best flight performance, try to keep payloads under 30 g . Secure your electronics using M3 screws, electrical tape, or both —tape alone works well for most builds, but using both provides maximum security. If any printed parts fit loosely, adjust the tolerances with a small amount of Scotch tape as needed. Finally, don't forget to add recovery wadding before every launch. MiniMoto Educational Drivetrain V1 (Competition Edition) A compact, fully functional educational drivetrain designed to demonstrate how power travels from the engine to the wheels. This model was designed for the Thangs "Keeping Busy - Toys & Projects" contest as a hands-on teaching tool that lets you see the internal workings of a vehicle drivetrain instead of hiding everything inside a transmission case. The assembly includes a working engine, selectable transmission, driveshaft, open differential, and rear axle. Every major component is removable, making it easy to understand how each system works individually and how they work together as a complete drivetrain. Whether you're learning about gear ratios, differential operation, or simply enjoy mechanical engineering, this model was built to make those concepts easy to visualize. As a bonus, assembling small mechanical models can be a relaxing way to focus your attention and take your mind off the day... unless you're fighting with a stubborn 3D printer. Apology I messed up. In my frantic rush to finish this model before the contest closed, I made the holes on the engine frame too big or too small the axles could slip out of the holes, and the control shaft wouldn't fit. This has since been fixed in a new file labeled "Frame_Fixed", but I had to delete the original model, already uploaded (and downloaded by 5 people) so I could add them. If you see double, this is the right one. I apologize for any confusion this caused and can only hope that you will be understanding of my situation. If you catch any more mistake I made, Please write a comment, I will try my best to fix them. Thank you. Features Working inline engine Selectable transmission with multiple gear ratios Functional open differential Rear axle and wheel assembly Modular design for easy assembly and maintenance Designed for education, demonstration, and display Parts Included Main Frame Front Axle Rear Axles Engine Frame Crankshaft Connecting Rods (x4) Piston Heads (x4) Transmission Control Shaft Transmission Frame Transmission High and Low Gears Transmission Power Shaft Transmission Shift Collar Transmission Transition Gear Ring Gear Spider Gears Wheels (x4) Tires (x4) Hardware Required None. The model is designed to assemble entirely from printed parts. Assembly Notes Most components use snap-fit / press-fit features designed to simplify assembly and reduce the need for hardware. (Glue may be required) Take your time during assembly and test-fit moving parts before fully snapping components together. Depending on your printer's tolerances, light sanding or minor cleanup may improve the fit of gears and shafts. Assembly instructions are at : https://thangs.com/designer/MINIMOTO_LAB/3d-model/MiniMoto%20Educational%20Drivetrain%20V1-Fixed-1571745 Tires and Rims are included but not required. Design Notes This project was designed to be both educational and enjoyable to assemble. Rather than hiding the drivetrain inside a solid body, the frame intentionally leaves the moving parts exposed so the complete path of power can be followed from the engine, through the transmission, into the differential, and finally to the wheels. The goal was not to create a scale vehicle, but to create an interactive model that makes mechanical concepts easy to see, understand, and demonstrate. description: UPDATE: Complete 40K 11th Edition Battlefield Terrain Set — Now with Optional Second Levels Take the Guesswork Out of Building a 40K Battlefield 40K 11th Edition introduced some excellent predetermined battlefield layouts that show players how to arrange the battlefield and where different terrain features should be placed. However, the dimensions of those terrain pieces are not always clearly provided, and determining what terrain to use can be surprisingly confusing. There are countless terrain models available, but figuring out which pieces you actually need, what sizes they should be, and how everything fits together on an 11th Edition battlefield can quickly become a project of its own. This collection was created to simplify that entire process. I carefully studied the battlefield layouts shown in the 40K app, determined the different terrain footprints and sizes needed to recreate them, and designed a complete, coordinated set that allows players to print everything required for a functional battlefield in one place. Instead of downloading unrelated models from multiple creators and hoping they work together, this set provides a clear starting point for new players and a convenient, consistent battlefield system for experienced players. I have also included A1 Mini print profiles, making the set accessible to players using smaller-format printers. UPDATE: Optional Second Levels Now Included I originally left second levels out of the terrain set intentionally. My goal was to keep the battlefield simple, easy to understand, and approachable for newer players who may already be learning a large number of rules. However, I also understand that many players want additional verticality and more options as they expand their battlefield. The collection now includes optional second-level components for anyone who wants to add elevated positions and more visual depth to the terrain. The second levels are completely optional. New players can continue using the original single-level terrain for the simplest possible setup, while more experienced players can add the upper levels wherever they want additional height and variety. This allows the terrain set to grow with you: Start with the simple, single-level battlefield Add second levels when you are ready Mix single-level and multi-level terrain on the same battlefield Customize the amount of verticality to match your preferred style of play The original goal remains unchanged: provide a battlefield that is easy to print, easy to understand, and ready to use without unnecessary complexity. What’s Included The complete collection includes: Battlefield terrain footprints Light terrain features Dense terrain features Optional second-level terrain components Standard objective markers Central and expansion objective markers Deployment zone markers Coordinated pieces designed to work together as one complete battlefield system A1 Mini-compatible print profiles The terrain footprints clearly define each terrain area, while the light and dense terrain pieces provide the physical structures needed to make the battlefield easy to understand and play on. The optional second levels allow players to add elevated positions without requiring everyone to use them. The objective and deployment zone markers make setup faster and reduce the need to repeatedly measure important locations before every game. AB, CD, EF, and GH Dense Terrain The dense terrain pieces were specifically designed and marked to correspond with the AB, CD, EF, and GH terrain categories shown in the battlefield layouts within the 40K app. This makes it much easier to identify which dense terrain piece belongs in each location when setting up a battlefield. Rather than comparing several similar-looking pieces, estimating dimensions, or trying to determine which terrain feature matches each layout position, simply select the appropriately marked AB, CD, EF, or GH model. This labeling system helps make battlefield setup faster, clearer, and more approachable—especially for players building their first complete terrain collection. Designed for Fast, Reliable Printing Every part of this collection was created with practical 3D printing in mind. The main design goals were: Fast print times Low filament use High printing success rates No support material required Simple, reliable geometry Easy battlefield setup Clear and consistent terrain sizes Minimal preparation after printing Optional expansion without unnecessary complexity The models were designed to print without supports and can be used immediately after removing them from the build plate. There should be no difficult support removal, complicated assembly, or extensive cleanup required. Print the pieces, remove them from the plate, and place them directly on the battlefield. The optional second levels can be added when desired, while the original single-level configuration remains available for players who prefer the simplest possible setup. These models are intended to be accessible to newer 3D-printer owners and players who may be building their first complete 40K battlefield. They are functional gaming pieces first—not overly complicated display models that require days of printing, large amounts of filament, or extensive post-processing. Recommended Printing Approach For the clearest gameplay experience, I recommend printing the footprints, light terrain, and dense terrain in different colors . Using separate colors makes it easier to quickly identify which terrain category a piece belongs to and helps reduce confusion when applying terrain rules during play. This is especially helpful for newer players, teaching games, or anyone trying to make battlefield interactions more intuitive at a glance. For example, using one color for footprints, another for light terrain, and another for dense terrain makes it easier to determine which terrain rules apply when models move into, through, around, or onto a terrain feature. The optional second-level pieces can be printed in the same color as the terrain category they belong to, helping them remain visually consistent with the rest of the battlefield. A Complete Starting Point for New Players This set is especially useful for someone who has recently started playing 40K and is asking: What terrain do I need? How large should each terrain area be? Which pieces are light terrain and which are dense terrain? Which dense terrain piece corresponds with AB, CD, EF, or GH? How do I reproduce the battlefield layouts shown in the app? Do I need second levels on my terrain? How many objective markers do I need? Where should deployment zones and objectives be placed? The answer regarding second levels is simple: use them when you want them . They are now included for players who want additional height and variety, but they are not required to begin using the terrain set. The goal is to remove as much uncertainty as possible so you can spend less time researching terrain and more time printing, painting, and playing. Modular and Easy to Customize The pieces can be printed as a complete matching set or mixed with terrain you already own. You can use the terrain entirely at ground level, add second levels to selected ruins, or create a battlefield with a mixture of single-level and multi-level structures. Terrain footprints can also be used with ruins, buildings, rock formations, industrial structures, or other decorative terrain placed within the marked areas. This makes the system useful even as your terrain collection grows. Print the included terrain for a quick, lightweight battlefield, or use the footprints, optional second levels, and markers as the foundation for a more detailed custom table. Additional Helpful Models Along with this terrain set, you may want something for taking quick measurements between models. I highly recommend this adjustable compass-style range finder by The Moose and Bolter: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2730760-kt-range-finder-the-ultimate-adjustable-compass#profileId-3026517 For tracking wounds, I also have several wound trackers listed here on MakerWorld. The model linked below was specifically designed to be lightweight and easy to print, just like this terrain set: https://makerworld.com/en/models/3011980-wound-tracker-engagement-range-gauge-11th-ed#profileId-3382976 Important Note This is an unofficial, community-created terrain and battlefield setup system intended for tabletop wargaming. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or produced by Games Workshop. Battlefield requirements, event standards, terrain interpretations, and tournament rulings may vary, so always confirm the requirements of your local gaming group or event organizer. The models are designed as a practical way to recreate and organize the battlefield layouts represented in the 40K app while making the process easier for players and 3D-printing hobbyists. Start with the simple single-level battlefield, add the optional second levels when you are ready, and play without the guesswork.

Axen vive en los canales tranquilos de Zoora, donde el agua casi nunca se mueve. Le gusta quedarse muy quieto en el fondo y observar cómo cambian las corrientes. Un día, después de una lluvia fuerte, el agua se volvió turbia y muchos pensaron que una entrada del camino antiguo había desaparecido bajo el barro. Axen no salió corriendo ni removió el agua. Se quedó quieto, esperando. Poco a poco, el barro bajó al fondo y entonces pudo ver algo que nadie había notado: una abertura de piedra seguía allí, escondida bajo tres pequeñas marcas azules. Así descubrió que la entrada no se había perdido. Solo estaba oculta. Desde entonces, cuando algo parece haber desaparecido en Zoora, muchos recuerdan a Axen y esperan un poco antes de rendirse. Moraleja: A veces, quedarse quieto es la mejor forma de ver las cosas con claridad.

Bluegill are a common species of freshwater gamefish native to the the United States east of the Rocky Mountains, but they have also been introduced to most of the other western states too. They're easy to catch and will bite on worms, artificial baits, corn, and even bread. For these reasons, bluegill are usually the first fish that young anglers in the US catch. Their exact coloration can vary between genders and seasons, but bluegill can typically be identified by their dark green bodies, black “ear” at the corner of the gill, reddish, orange chest, and their blue chins and gills. They are usually at the bottom of the food chain and are preyed on by bass, pike, catfish, herons, and other aquatic predators. To defend themselves they have sharp spines poking out from their dorsal fins that teach the young anglers who catch them to be careful when unhooking them. For this model, the pectoral fins are printed separately to maximize strength and then glued into the slots behind the gills. I used bronze silk PLA for most of the body, but a dark olive green PLA might match the real coloration more closely.
